title: Ester saponification
subtitle: Hydroxide adds, methoxide leaves, and a proton transfer makes the carboxylate

reactants.caption: methyl acetate + sodium hydroxide
hintTiers: Which carbon of the ester is electron-poor: the carbonyl carbon or the methyl carbons?
The hydroxide lone pair forms a bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydroxide lone pair → new O–C bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: lp O6 -> σ O6-C2; σ C2-O4 -> lp O4
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: At a C=O carbon the nucleophile adds first and the π bond moves onto oxygen. Methoxide leaves in a separate step.
SN2 on the methyl group with carboxylate leaving does happen, but very rarely. Hydroxide attacks the much more electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
Both oxygens are electron-rich. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon. Now move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

tetrahedral.caption: tetrahedral intermediate
hintTiers: The oxygen anion re-forms C=O. Two groups could leave: hydroxide or methoxide. Which gives a new product?
Re-form the C=O π bond from the oxygen anion, and break the bond to the OMe oxygen. Two arrows.
Oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond; C–OMe bond → lone pair on the methoxy oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing hydroxide just goes back to the ester. Methoxide and hydroxide are similar leaving groups; losing methoxide moves the reaction forwards.
Moving the proton from one oxygen to the other changes nothing useful. Collapse the intermediate: re-form C=O and lose a group.

acid-and-methoxide.caption: acetic acid + methoxide
hintTiers: Methoxide is a strong base (pKa of methanol about 16). How acidic is a carboxylic acid?
The methoxide lone pair takes the O–H proton of the acid; the O–H bonding pair stays on the acid oxygen. Two arrows.
Methoxide lone pair → new O–H bond to the acid proton; acid O–H bond → lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Methoxide could add again, but the proton transfer is much faster and goes downhill: carboxylic acids have pKa about 5.
That carbon has no leaving group. Methoxide is a strong base: what is the most acidic proton here?

steps.explanationAfterStep: Hydroxide adds to the carbonyl carbon: a tetrahedral intermediate with three oxygens on one carbon.
The C=O bond re-forms and methoxide leaves. Up to here every step is reversible.

Methoxide (methanol pKa about 16) takes the proton from acetic acid (pKa about 5). The carboxylate cannot be attacked by methanol, so this step makes saponification irreversible. Acid work-up gives acetic acid.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide adds to the carbonyl carbon of methyl acetate. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses and methoxide leaves, giving acetic acid. Methoxide removes its proton: the carboxylate is so stable that this last step makes the whole hydrolysis irreversible.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 10
